claim: GCC185 is predicted to be almost entirely coiled-coil, perhaps >200 nm in length.
source: Secondary structure prediction algorithms (Lupas et al., 1991) suggest that GCC185 may be almost entirely coiled-coil, perhaps >200 nm in length.
evidence: Based on computational prediction using established algorithms cited in the literature

claim: GCC185 wild type protein migrates at ~220 kD upon SDS-PAGE.
source: The wild type protein migrated at ~220 kD upon SDS-PAGE; GCC185 △hinge was somewhat smaller (Figure 2A).
evidence: Experimental observation shown in Figure 2A

claim: GCC185 △hinge protein is somewhat smaller than wild type upon SDS-PAGE.
source: The wild type protein migrated at ~220 kD upon SDS-PAGE; GCC185 △hinge was somewhat smaller (Figure 2A).
evidence: Experimental observation shown in Figure 2A

claim: GCC185 is a parallel dimer of ~145 nm in length with splayed ends under physiological buffer conditions.
source: AFM of GCC185 under physiological buffer conditions revealed the molecule as a parallel dimer of ~145 nm in length with splayed ends (Figure 2B,D; Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1–3).
evidence: Direct measurement by atomic force microscopy under physiological conditions

claim: GCC185 contains numerous cysteine residues.
source: GCC185 contains numerous cysteine residues (Figure 3—figure supplement 1,2)
evidence: Shown in supplementary figures

claim: Dithiothreitol is important to mimic the reducing environment of the cytoplasm for GCC185 experiments.
source: it was important to include dithiothreitol to mimic the reducing environment of the cytoplasm for all experiments.
evidence: Based on understanding of cellular biochemistry and experimental design

claim: Eighty five percent of GCC185 molecules show splaying of at least one end of the dimeric coiled coil.
source: Eighty five percent of the molecules showed splaying of at least one end of the dimeric coiled coil, and 38% showed splaying of both ends (Figure 3).
evidence: Quantitative analysis of AFM images

claim: 38% of GCC185 molecules show splaying of both ends.
source: Eighty five percent of the molecules showed splaying of at least one end of the dimeric coiled coil, and 38% showed splaying of both ends (Figure 3).
evidence: Quantitative analysis of AFM images

claim: The N-terminal GFP used in AFM experiments did not impede the ability of the N-terminus to form a coiled coil.
source: It is important to note that the N-terminal GFP used in AFM experiments did not impede the ability of the N-terminus to form a coiled coil because many fewer splays and central bubbles were seen in initial experiments when GCC185 was purified in the absence of dithiothreitol (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Comparison of experimental conditions with and without DTT

claim: Without DTT, GCC185 appeared rod-like.
source: Without DTT, GCC185 appeared rod-like.
evidence: Experimental observation under specific conditions

claim: Half of the GCC185 molecules display central unwinding of the coiled coil structure.
source: Remarkably, half of the GCC185 molecules displayed central unwinding of the coiled coil structure (Figures 2,3).
evidence: Quantitative analysis of AFM images

claim: Such unwinding in a coiled coil has not been detected previously.
source: To our knowledge, such unwinding in a coiled coil has not been detected previously.
evidence: Authors' assessment of existing literature

claim: The unwound 'bubble' region was less frequently observed in GCC185 △hinge protein preparations.
source: The unwound 'bubble' region was less frequently observed in GCC185 △hinge protein preparations (Figure 2C,D)
evidence: Comparative analysis of wild type and mutant proteins by AFM

claim: The mean size of the bubble was ~27 nm in wild type versus ~17 nm in △hinge molecules.
source: the mean size of the bubble was ~27 nm in wild type versus ~17 nm in △hinge molecules, with a much sharper size distribution in the latter case, and only 20% of the △hinge molecules showing any bubble at all (Figure 2C,E).
evidence: Quantitative measurements from AFM images

claim: Only 20% of the △hinge molecules show any bubble at all.
source: the mean size of the bubble was ~27 nm in wild type versus ~17 nm in △hinge molecules, with a much sharper size distribution in the latter case, and only 20% of the △hinge molecules showing any bubble at all (Figure 2C,E).
evidence: Quantitative analysis of AFM images

claim: △hinge proteins all showed the longest mean, normalized splay-to-splay distances.
source: △hinge proteins all showed the longest mean, normalized splay-to-splay distances; using this metric, wild type molecules with bubbles were more bent than those without bubbles (Figure 2F).
evidence: Quantitative analysis of molecular conformations from AFM data

claim: Wild type molecules with bubbles were more bent than those without bubbles.
source: △hinge proteins all showed the longest mean, normalized splay-to-splay distances; using this metric, wild type molecules with bubbles were more bent than those without bubbles (Figure 2F).
evidence: Quantitative analysis of molecular conformations from AFM data

claim: GCC185 is a flexible molecule and its tendency to bend is contributed by the so-called 'hinge' residues 751-805 and 890-939.
source: These data show that GCC185 is a flexible molecule and its tendency to bend is contributed by the so-called 'hinge' residues 751-805 and 890-939.
evidence: Inference from comparative analysis of wild type and hinge deletion mutant

claim: The molecules detected by AFM represent individual dimers rather than end-to-end tetramers.
source: That the molecules detected by AFM represent individual dimers rather than end-to-end tetramers was determined by introduction of an HA epitope tag into the central hinge region (Figure 4A); antibody labeling of such molecules was readily detected by AFM and showed antibodies at the position expected for the epitope tag location within a parallel dimer (Figure 4B-D).
evidence: Epitope tagging and antibody labeling experiments visualized by AFM

claim: Purified GFP-FLAG-GCC185 has an overall mean length of ~145 nm.
source: AFM also revealed that purified GFP-FLAG-GCC185 has an overall mean length of ~145 nm (Figure 3—figure supplement 1,2,4).
evidence: Direct measurement by AFM

claim: The N-terminal half of GCC185 (1-889) was longer than half the length of the complete protein (mean length = 91.2 nm).
source: the N-terminal half of GCC185 (1-889) was longer than half the length of the complete protein (mean length = 91.2 nm; Figure 3— figure supplement 2, 4).
evidence: Measurement of protein fragment by AFM

claim: The sum of the lengths of GCC185 fragments could account for the length of the full-length protein determined by AFM.
source: The sum of the lengths of GCC185 fragments could account for the length of the full-length protein determined by AFM.
evidence: Comparison of fragment lengths with full-length protein

claim: Full-length GCC185 and all fragments were ~30% shorter than the predicted lengths for coiled-coils with the same number of residues.
source: However, full-length GCC185 and all fragments were ~30% shorter than the predicted lengths for coiled-coils with the same number of residues (the cartoons in Figure 3—figure supplement 1,2 are drawn to scale for each portion of the molecules and summarized in Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Comparison of measured lengths with predicted lengths

claim: GCC185's N-terminus contains more coiled coil than the C-terminal half.
source: These data indicate that GCC185's N-terminus contains more coiled coil than the C-terminal half, and the entire protein contains less total coiled-coil structure than originally predicted.
evidence: Inference from length measurements of protein fragments

claim: The entire GCC185 protein contains less total coiled-coil structure than originally predicted.
source: These data indicate that GCC185's N-terminus contains more coiled coil than the C-terminal half, and the entire protein contains less total coiled-coil structure than originally predicted.
evidence: Inference from comparison of measured and predicted lengths

claim: Immunoblots confirmed ~85% depletion of endogenous GCC185 protein in siRNA experiments.
source: In these experiments, immunoblots confirmed ~85% depletion of endogenous GCC185 protein (Figure 5B inset).
evidence: Quantification of immunoblot data

claim: In GCC185-depleted cells, MPRs were detected in numerous, peripheral transport intermediates.
source: As expected, in depleted cells, MPRs were detected in numerous, peripheral transport intermediates; the Golgi ribbon was also dispersed (Figure 5A,B; Hayes et al., 2009; Reddy, 2006; Brown et al., 2011).
evidence: Microscopy observations consistent with previous studies

claim: In GCC185-depleted cells, the Golgi ribbon was dispersed.
source: As expected, in depleted cells, MPRs were detected in numerous, peripheral transport intermediates; the Golgi ribbon was also dispersed (Figure 5A,B; Hayes et al., 2009; Reddy, 2006; Brown et al., 2011).
evidence: Microscopy observations consistent with previous studies

claim: The GCC185-depletion phenotype was readily reversed in cells co-expressing an siRNA-resistant Myc-GCC185 protein.
source: This phenotype was readily reversed in cells co-expressing an siRNA-resistant Myc-GCC185 protein (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: Rescue experiment results

claim: Much less rescue was detected when the △hinge mutant protein was tested for rescue capacity.
source: In contrast, much less rescue was detected when the △hinge mutant protein, expressed at the same level (Figure 5C), was tested for rescue capacity (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: Quantitative comparison of rescue experiments

claim: A protein in which putative hinge sequences were replaced with unstructured gly-gly-ser repeats of the same length was fully capable of rescuing both transport vesicle receipt and normal Golgi morphology.
source: Moreover, a protein in which putative hinge sequences were replaced with unstructured gly-gly-ser repeats of the same length (Figure 1) was fully capable of rescuing both transport vesicle receipt and normal Golgi morphology (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: Rescue experiment with flexible linker replacement

claim: All three myc-tagged rescue constructs were expressed at similar levels in the individual scored cells.
source: Quantification verified that all three myc-tagged, rescue constructs were expressed at similar levels in the individual, scored cells (Figure 5C; overall rescue construct transfection efficiency 60%), at no more than 3-5 fold the level of the endogenous protein for the total pool of cells.
evidence: Quantitative analysis of protein expression levels

claim: Hinge sequences are important for GCC185-mediated vesicle tethering.
source: These experiments demonstrate the importance of hinge sequences for GCC185-mediated vesicle tethering, and show that these sequences provide flexibility rather than a binding site for another cellular component.
evidence: Inference from rescue experiments comparing deletion and flexible replacement

claim: Hinge sequences provide flexibility rather than a binding site for another cellular component.
source: These experiments demonstrate the importance of hinge sequences for GCC185-mediated vesicle tethering, and show that these sequences provide flexibility rather than a binding site for another cellular component.
evidence: Inference from the fact that flexible linker replacement rescues function

claim: PLA signal was readily detected on Golgi complexes using mouse anti-GCC185 N-terminus and rabbit anti-GCC185 C-terminus antibodies.
source: Using mouse anti-GCC185 N-terminus and rabbit anti-GCC185 C-terminus antibodies, PLA signal was readily detected on Golgi complexes of individual cells (Figure 6A).
evidence: Proximity ligation assay results

claim: No PLA signal was obtained using mouse anti-Golgin 245 C-terminus and rabbit anti-GCC185 C-terminus antibodies.
source: In contrast, no signal was obtained using mouse anti-Golgin 245 C-terminus and rabbit anti-GCC185 C-terminus antibodies, even though both proteins are localized to the trans Golgi network.
evidence: Negative control experiment for PLA specificity

claim: Mouse anti-cis-Golgi GM130 antibodies yielded only a very weak PLA signal when used in combination with rabbit anti-GCC185 antibodies.
source: Similarly, mouse anti-cis-Golgi GM130 antibodies yielded only a very weak PLA signal when used in combination with rabbit anti-GCC185 antibodies.
evidence: Control experiment for PLA specificity

claim: GCC185's N- and C-termini are within <40 nm of each other on the Golgi in cells.
source: Quantification of the PLA data confirmed specific PLA labeling for reactions with the GCC185 N- and C-terminal domain antibodies (Figure 6B), consistent with proximity of the N- and C-termini of this protein on the Golgi in cells.
evidence: Proximity ligation assay results indicating spatial proximity

claim: GFP-GCC185-△hinge yielded a significantly weaker PLA signal when compared with cells expressing GFP-GCC185.
source: However, GFP-GCC185-△hinge yielded a significantly weaker PLA signal when compared with cells expressing GFP-GCC185 (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: Quantitative comparison of PLA signals between wild type and mutant

claim: The flexibility-conferring regions facilitate the ability of the N- and C-termini to achieve proximity on the Golgi.
source: This suggests strongly that the flexibility-conferring regions facilitate the ability of the N- and C-termini to achieve proximity on the Golgi.
evidence: Inference from comparison of PLA signals between wild type and hinge deletion mutant

claim: At high expression levels of GCC185-△hinge, proximity signals likely represent inter- rather than intra-molecular processes.
source: Only at higher expression levels was proximity detected for the GCC185-△hinge construct; at high expression levels, these are likely to represent inter- rather than intra-molecular processes.
evidence: Interpretation of PLA data at different expression levels

claim: The presence of a flexible region is needed for GCC185 function.
source: These experiments show that the presence of a flexible region is needed for GCC185 function and permits the N- and C-termini to become closer together, on the Golgi, in cells.
evidence: Summary of PLA and rescue experiments

claim: The flexible region permits the N- and C-termini to become closer together, on the Golgi, in cells.
source: These experiments show that the presence of a flexible region is needed for GCC185 function and permits the N- and C-termini to become closer together, on the Golgi, in cells.
evidence: Summary of PLA experiments

claim: Vesicles carrying GFP-Rab9 were captured by GCC185 N-terminal residues 1-358 but not by internal residues 1032–1331.
source: Figures 7B-D show that vesicles were indeed captured by the N-terminal 1–358 fragment but not by the internal fragment of similar length.
evidence: In vitro vesicle capture assay results

claim: The 1–358 sequences tethered most effectively when the obligate GST dimer was located at the fragment's C-terminus (1–358-GST) rather than the N-terminus (GST-1–358).
source: Interestingly, the 1–358 sequences tethered most effectively when the obligate GST dimer was located at the fragment's C-terminus (1–358-GST) rather than the N-terminus (GST-1–358; Figure 7C).
evidence: Comparison of vesicle capture efficiency with different GST positions

claim: Neither early endosome (EEA1) nor endoplasmic reticulum (calnexin) markers were captured by the GCC185 constructs tested.
source: Specificity control experiments showed that neither early endosome (EEA1) nor endoplasmic reticulum (calnexin) markers were captured by the constructs tested (Figure 7C).
evidence: Negative control experiments for vesicle capture specificity

claim: N-terminal sequences are essential for GCC185 function in cells.
source: N-terminal sequences are essential for GCC185 function in cells (Hayes et al., 2009), consistent with their ability to bind transport vesicles in vitro.
evidence: Previous study cited and consistency with current in vitro data

claim: The fragment capable of splaying at the N-terminus (1–358-GST) showed highest tethering activity.
source: The functional significance of N-terminal splaying detected in 80% of purified GCC185 molecules (Figure 2,3) is confirmed by the finding that the fragment capable of splaying at the N-terminus (1–358-GST) showed highest tethering activity (Figure 7C,D).
evidence: Correlation between structural feature and functional activity

claim: Free N-termini represent both the active and most abundant form of GCC185.
source: Although we cannot rule out completely, the possibility of GST-steric hindrance for vesicle binding when present at the N-terminus, these data suggest that free N-termini represent both the active and most abundant form of this tethering protein.
evidence: Inference from structural and functional data, with acknowledgment of alternative explanation

claim: GCC185 N-terminal sequences can bind cargo.
source: These experiments show that GCC185 N-terminal sequences can bind cargo—essential for a bona fide tethering protein.
evidence: Summary of vesicle capture experiments

claim: This represents the first direct demonstration of in vitro vesicle tethering by a TGN localized, GRIP-domain containing tethering protein.
source: Moreover, this represents the first direct demonstration of in vitro vesicle tethering by a TGN localized, GRIP-domain containing tethering protein.
evidence: Authors' assessment of novelty relative to existing literature

claim: Flexibility in a tethering protein is required for its functionality in cells.
source: We have shown, for the first time, that flexibility in a tethering protein is required for its functionality in cells, both in supporting the receipt of transport vesicles at the Golgi and maintaining Golgi ribbon structure.
evidence: Summary of rescue experiments with hinge deletion and flexible replacement

claim: Transport vesicles can bind to GCC185's N-terminus.
source: We have shown that transport vesicles can bind to GCC185's N-terminus, and seem to prefer to bind to splayed ends of this dimeric, coiled coil tether.
evidence: Summary of vesicle capture experiments

claim: Transport vesicles seem to prefer to bind to splayed ends of GCC185.
source: We have shown that transport vesicles can bind to GCC185's N-terminus, and seem to prefer to bind to splayed ends of this dimeric, coiled coil tether.
evidence: Inference from comparison of tethering activity with different GST positions

claim: GCC185 is C-terminally anchored to the TGN through Rab6 and Arl1 GTPases.
source: Our data favor a model whereby GCC185 is C-terminally anchored to the TGN through Rab6 and Arl1 GTPases (Burguete et al., 2008)
evidence: Previous study cited

claim: GCC185 captures Rab9-decorated transport vesicles.
source: Our data favor a model whereby GCC185 is C-terminally anchored to the TGN through Rab6 and Arl1 GTPases (Burguete et al., 2008) and captures Rab9-decorated transport vesicles (Hayes et al., 2009; Reddy, 2006)
evidence: Previous studies cited

claim: The central bubble gives significant flexibility to GCC185 and would allow it to collapse onto the Golgi surface.
source: importantly, the central bubble gives significant flexibility to the protein and would allow it to collapse onto the Golgi surface, bringing vesicles close to the trans Golgi target membrane (Figure 8).
evidence: Inference from structural data and functional implications

claim: GCC185 can bind multiple Rab GTPases along its length.
source: GCC185 can bind multiple Rab GTPases along its length (Hayes et al., 2009), as well as syntaxin16, Arl1 and Arl4 GTPases (Burguete et al., 2008; Ganley et al., 2008; Lin et al., 2011).
evidence: Multiple previous studies cited

claim: GCC185 binds to syntaxin16, Arl1 and Arl4 GTPases.
source: GCC185 can bind multiple Rab GTPases along its length (Hayes et al., 2009), as well as syntaxin16, Arl1 and Arl4 GTPases (Burguete et al., 2008; Ganley et al., 2008; Lin et al., 2011).
evidence: Multiple previous studies cited

claim: GCC185 binds to CLASP proteins that catalyze microtubule polymerization from the Golgi surface.
source: GCC185 also binds to CLASP proteins that catalyze microtubule polymerization from the Golgi surface (Efimov et al., 2007).
evidence: Previous study cited

claim: GCC185 residues 938–1032 comprise an AP-1 binding site that is needed for GCC185 vesicle tethering.
source: In previous work (Brown et al., 2011), we showed that GCC185 residues 938–1032 comprise an AP-1 binding site that is also needed for GCC185 vesicle tethering (blue bar in Figure 1A)
evidence: Previous study by the same authors

claim: The transport vesicles captured by GCC185 are AP-1 decorated.
source: the transport vesicles are AP-1 decorated, thus this was presumed to represent a possible vesicle binding site.
evidence: Characterization of vesicles and inference about binding

claim: A Rab9 GTPase binding site is located directly between the two deletions made to generate the △hinge mutant.
source: Moreover, an apparently dispensible, Rab9 GTPase binding site is located directly between the two deletions made to generate the △hinge mutant (orange bar, Figure 1A).
evidence: Structural annotation based on previous characterization

claim: Both Rab9 and AP-1 are present on the transport vesicles captured by GCC185.
source: Both Rab9 and AP-1 are present on the transport vesicles captured, but we do not yet know the precise molecular interaction underlying the ability of the N-terminal domain to bind vesicles.
evidence: Characterization of captured vesicles

claim: The tether gains efficiency by avidity through splayed N-terminus.
source: That a splayed N-terminus is utilized suggests that the tether gains efficiency by avidity, and can reach out to 'hug' the vesicle.
evidence: Inference from structural features and functional data

claim: The AP-1 binding site (939–1,031) is essential for GCC185's role in vesicle tethering but not Golgi ribbon maintenance.
source: The AP-1 binding site (939–1,031)is essential for GCC185's role in vesicle tethering but not Golgi ribbon maintenance (Brown et al., 2011), and must be considered in any model of GCC185 vesicle tethering.
evidence: Previous study by the same authors

claim: Golgin-245 shares with GCC185 two very obvious breaks in the coiled coil that may also form a central bubble.
source: Like GCC185, the other human GRIP domain Golgins are also predicted to contain a high proportion of coiled coil sequences. Golgin-245 shares with GCC185 two very obvious breaks in the coiled coil that may also form a central bubble; its absolute N-terminus is also likely splayed.
evidence: Sequence analysis and prediction based on similarity to GCC185

claim: Golgin-245's absolute N-terminus is also likely splayed.
source: Golgin-245 shares with GCC185 two very obvious breaks in the coiled coil that may also form a central bubble; its absolute N-terminus is also likely splayed.
evidence: Prediction based on sequence analysis and similarity to GCC185

claim: Golgin-97 and GCC88 proteins are likely about half as long as GCC185 by sequence alone.
source: The shorter Golgin-97 and GCC88 proteins are likely about half as long as GCC185 by sequence alone
evidence: Sequence comparison

claim: Golgin-97's N-terminus is likely splayed.
source: Golgin-97's N-terminus is likely splayed, and GCC88 may very well also contain a central bubble.
evidence: Prediction based on sequence analysis and similarity to GCC185

claim: GCC88 may very well also contain a central bubble.
source: Golgin-97's N-terminus is likely splayed, and GCC88 may very well also contain a central bubble.
evidence: Prediction based on sequence analysis and similarity to GCC185

claim: A domain between GCC185 residues 1332 and 1438 is required for maintenance of Golgi ribbon structure but not transport vesicle tethering.
source: Finally, a domain between GCC185 residues 1332 and 1438 is required for maintenance of Golgi ribbon structure but not transport vesicle tethering (Brown et al., 2011).
evidence: Previous study by the same authors

claim: Simple engagement of N- and C-termini is not sufficient for both vesicle capture and Golgi ribbon stabilization.
source: This observation highlights the fact that workers in this field have oversimplified thinking about how tethers function—simple engagement of N- and C-termini is not sufficient for both vesicle capture and Golgi ribbon stabilization.
evidence: Inference from the finding that separate domains control different functions

claim: GCC185 could not tether vesicles upon re-localization to mitochondria in a previous study.
source: A recent paper studying Golgi tethers (Wong and Munro, 2014) concluded that unlike other TGN tethers, GCC185 could not tether vesicles upon re-localization to mitochondria.
evidence: Previous study cited

claim: The Wong and Munro study may have assayed the ability of TGN tethers to recruit/assemble TGN ribbons, rather than capture rare transport vesicle intermediates.
source: It is very possible that that study assayed the ability of TGN tethers to recruit/assemble TGN ribbons, rather than capture rare transport vesicle intermediates.
evidence: Authors' interpretation of another study's results

claim: Ribbon assembly and transport vesicle capture are driven by separate domains of GCC185.
source: Since ribbon assembly and transport vesicle capture are driven by separate domains of GCC185, perhaps GCC185 is more potent in vesicle tethering rather than Golgi ribbon assembly.
evidence: Inference from previous functional domain mapping

claim: The floppy appearance of purified GCC185 argues against this protein behaving like a pipe cleaner protruding on the surface of the trans Golgi network in cells.
source: Whatever the explanation, the floppy appearance of purified GCC185, when deposited on mica in the absence of fixative, and the proximity of GCC185's N- and C-termini on the Golgi in cells, argue strongly against this protein behaving like a pipe cleaner, protruding on the surface of the trans Golgi network in cells.
evidence: Inference from AFM structural data and PLA proximity data

claim: Tether collapse represents an appealing alternative model to the rigid extended rod model.
source: Instead, tether collapse represents an appealing, alternative model.
evidence: Authors' interpretation of all data presented

claim: GCC185 is a Golgin required for the transport of mannose 6-phosphate receptors (MPRs) from late endosomes to the trans Golgi network.
source: GCC185 is a Golgin required for the transport of mannose 6-phosphate receptors (MPRs) from late endosomes to the trans Golgi network (Reddy, 2006; Derby et al., 2007).
evidence: Previous studies cited

claim: Cells depleted of GCC185 accumulate MPRs in Rab9 GTPase- and AP-1-decorated transport carriers.
source: Cells depleted of GCC185 accumulate MPRs in Rab9 GTPase- and AP-1-decorated transport carriers (Hayes et al., 2009; Reddy, 2006; Brown et al., 2011), providing an assay for GCC185 tethering capacity.
evidence: Previous studies cited

claim: GCC185 is likely anchored on the TGN surface by cooperative binding of its C-terminus to both Rab6 and Arl1 GTPases.
source: GCC185 is likely anchored on the TGN surface by cooperative binding of its C-terminus to both Rab6 and Arl1 GTPases (Burguete et al., 2008).
evidence: Previous study cited

claim: GCC185 binds Arl1 rather weakly, but Rab6A binding greatly enhances Arl1 interaction.
source: We (Reddy, 2006; Burguete et al., 2008) and others (Derby, 2004) have shown that GCC185 binds Arl1 rather weakly, but Rab6A binding greatly enhances Arl1 interaction (Burguete et al., 2008).
evidence: Multiple previous studies cited

claim: 90% depletion of Arl1 is required to displace GCC185 from membranes and to detect its role in Golgi localization of the GCC185 C-terminus.
source: in fact, 90% depletion of Arl1 is required to displace GCC185 from membranes and to detect its role in Golgi localization of the GCC185 C-terminus (Burguete et al., 2008).
evidence: Previous study cited

claim: Membrane trafficking involves the collection of cargo into transport vesicles, movement of vesicles along cytoskeletal tracks, and tethering, docking and fusion of vesicles at their target membranes.
source: Membrane trafficking involves the collection of cargo into transport vesicles, movement of vesicles along cytoskeletal tracks, and tethering, docking and fusion of vesicles at their target membranes.
evidence: General knowledge about membrane trafficking

claim: Tethering is the process by which partner membranes are brought together into close proximity to permit their subsequent fusion.
source: Tethering is the process by which partner membranes are brought together into close proximity to permit their subsequent fusion (Pfeffer, 1999; Sztul and Lupashin, 2006; Yu and Hughson, 2010).
evidence: Definition from previous literature

claim: Two classes of transport vesicle tethers have been described: multi-subunit complexes and larger, dimeric coiled-coil containing proteins.
source: Two classes of transport vesicle tethers have been described to date: multi-subunit complexes such as the Exocyst, COG, Dsl1 and TRAPP complexes (Bröcker et al., 2010), and larger, dimeric coiled-coil containing proteins such as p115 and EEA1 (Sztul and Lupashin, 2006; Munro, 2011).
evidence: Classification from previous literature

claim: Both classes of tethers share the ability to bind to Rab GTPases, SNARE proteins and vesicle coat complexes.
source: Both classes share the ability to bind to Rab GTPases, SNARE proteins and vesicle coat complexes, suggesting that they play important roles in coordinating molecular events important for target recognition and membrane fusion (Short et al., 2005; Cai et al., 2007; Sinka et al., 2008; Hayes et al., 2009; Hughson and Reinisch, 2010).
evidence: Summary of findings from multiple previous studies

claim: Golgins are long, Golgi-associated proteins that contain a high proportion of sequences that are predicted to form coiled coils.
source: Golgins are long, Golgi-associated proteins that contain a high proportion of sequences that are predicted to form coiled coils (Munro, 2011; Short et al., 2005).
evidence: General characterization from previous literature

claim: Golgins are anchored to the Golgi via their C-termini.
source: They are anchored to the Golgi via their C-termini, and models suggest that they protrude long distances, relying on the relative rigidity of the coiled coil structure to provide a meshwork that can capture vesicles in the vicinity of the Golgi (Yu and Hughson, 2010; Munro, 2011).
evidence: General knowledge from previous literature

claim: Previous models suggest that Golgins protrude long distances, relying on the relative rigidity of the coiled coil structure to provide a meshwork that can capture vesicles.
source: They are anchored to the Golgi via their C-termini, and models suggest that they protrude long distances, relying on the relative rigidity of the coiled coil structure to provide a meshwork that can capture vesicles in the vicinity of the Golgi (Yu and Hughson, 2010; Munro, 2011).
evidence: Previous models from literature
